title: Party Invite Phishing Scams Are the New Missed Connections
gist: Fake Evite/Paperless Post party-invite phishing emails, flagged by an FTC consumer alert in May 2026, are spreading from compromised accounts even with two-factor authentication enabled. As an unintended side effect, recipients checking whether the invites are real are reviving dormant friendships. The article is a culture piece rather than a security analysis; its hard data is the FBI's $21B in 2025 scam losses and research on social withdrawal.

insights.claim: Scammers are impersonating event-invitation platforms such as Evite and Paperless Post, sending fake invites that ask recipients to enter their email username and password, or a phone number and a special code, to see event details or RSVP. The FTC issued a consumer alert about the scheme in May 2026 after receiving more reports.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Trusted consumer SaaS brands are being turned into credential-harvesting lures. Watch for brand-trust damage to invitation platforms and for demand for email and phishing-defense tools.

insights.claim: A victim whose account sent fake Paperless Post invites to contacts from 15 years earlier had two-factor authentication enabled. Standard consumer account-security measures did not stop the compromise.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: This supports demand for stronger authentication, such as phishing-resistant methods beyond basic 2FA, and for account-takeover detection.

insights.claim: Email phishing has grown more sophisticated through social engineering: it creates urgency or fear and exploits personal relationships (spear phishing). AI has made these deceptions harder to detect.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: AI-assisted phishing strengthens the case for continued spending on email security and identity protection.

insights.so_what: The size of the fraud-loss pool shows how big the market for anti-fraud, identity, and scam-detection products could be.

insights.claim: Fake party invites are having an unintended social effect. Recipients contact the supposed sender to check whether the invite is real, which rekindles dormant relationships. One victim reconnected with several old friends and colleagues, including a former coworker he had not spoken to in over a decade.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: This is a counterintuitive, low-stakes use case for connection products: a low-friction excuse to get in touch drives reconnection.

insights.claim: Only about 30 percent of people contact an old friend even when researchers make it as easy as possible. A scam provides 'social cover' that motivates people to reach out, according to Simon Fraser University psychology professor Lara Aknin.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Hesitance to reach out is a large behavioral barrier. Products that give users a legitimate pretext to reconnect may address demand that is currently going unmet.
insights.quote: the scam provides a legitimate excuse or social cover to do so

insights.claim: A 2024 Communications Psychology study of 2,400 adults in the US, UK, and Canada found that people avoid contacting old friends because they expect the other person won't want to hear from them or fear awkwardness. It also found that North America's high priority on work and productivity has led people to cut social time.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: Structural loneliness, driven by work demands, supports long-term demand for social and community platforms.

insights.claim: Close relationships are shrinking: nearly half of the population (44 percent) has five or fewer acquaintances, according to the article.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: This is a data point for the loneliness-economy thesis behind social and connection-focused consumer tech.
